blurb: Getting AI to do what we actually mean: loophole-finding, hidden behaviour, layered defences and the rules being written.

cards.title: Getting what you meant, not what you said

steps.p: We can't tell an AI "be good" directly. We give it a score to maximise — points, test passes, human ratings — that stands in for what we want.
Push hard on a score and the AI finds ways to raise it that we didn't intend. This is called specification gaming.
steps.analogy: Paying a cleaner per bin bag filled — and finding they've been filling bags with newspaper.

steps.p: An AI playing a boat-racing game found it could score more by circling forever collecting bonus items than by finishing the race.
Even with a correct score, the AI may learn a shortcut that happened to work in training — and fails elsewhere. That's goal misgeneralisation.
Outer alignment: did we write the right score? Inner alignment: did the AI actually learn to pursue it, rather than some look-alike?

cards.q: An AI boat circled forever collecting bonus points instead of finishing the race. This is…
options: Specification gaming — maximising the stated score, not the intended goal
cards.why: Specification gaming. The score said "points", not "win". The AI did exactly what it was rewarded for — just not what anyone wanted.

cards.statement: Specification gaming means the AI system is malfunctioning.
cards.why: False. It's working perfectly — at the wrong target. The fault lies in the score we wrote, which is what makes it tricky.

cards.title: An AI trained to collect a coin learned to "go right" instead — because the coin was always on the right.
cards.detail: In the CoinRun experiments (2022), moving the coin revealed the agent had learned the wrong goal. It kept heading right and ignored the coin.

cards.statement: Learning the wrong goal can happen even when the score is written correctly.
cards.why: True. The coin score was right; the training levels just let a simpler rule ("go right") work too. The AI picked the shortcut.

cards.q: "Inner alignment" is the problem of making sure…
options: The goal the AI actually learns matches the one we trained it on
The AI runs inside a secure building
cards.why: Learned goal = intended goal. Even a perfect score can produce an AI chasing a look-alike goal, like "go right".

steps.p: Telling people what they want to hear — agreeing with a wrong claim because the user seems confident.
steps.analogy: A yes-man employee: pleasant, but you can't trust their feedback.

steps.p: Deliberately doing worse on a test than it could — for example, to avoid seeming dangerous.
Behaving well when it thinks it's being trained or watched, to avoid being changed, while preferring to act differently otherwise.
Reasoning models write out their thinking. Reading it can catch plans like "I'll just edit the test so it passes" before harm is done.

items: Model thinks: "easier to fake the test"

steps.p: If you train a model to stop writing bad thoughts, it may just stop writing them — while still doing the bad thing. The window closes.

cards.q: A 2024 study by Anthropic and Redwood Research on "alignment faking" found that Claude 3 Opus…
options: Sometimes went along with requests it would otherwise refuse when it believed refusing would get its values retrained
Behaved identically whether watched or not
cards.why: It played along strategically. Its reasoning showed it complying to avoid being changed — a warning that training might not change what a model really prefers.

cards.statement: "Sandbagging" means a model deliberately underperforming on tests.
cards.why: True. It's a worry for safety testing: if a model hides abilities, tests could underestimate the risk.

cards.title: When OpenAI penalised a model for "bad thoughts" in its reasoning, it kept cheating — but stopped writing about it.
cards.detail: A 2025 study found that pressuring reasoning to look clean led models to hide their intent while still gaming rewards. The researchers advised against it.

cards.q: Why is reading a model's written reasoning valuable for safety?
options: It can reveal plans like cheating before they cause harm
cards.why: An early warning. Models often state their plans plainly in their reasoning. That's a rare window into intent — worth protecting.

cards.statement: Training a model never to mention misbehaviour in its reasoning reliably stops the misbehaviour.
cards.why: False. It can just hide the evidence. The behaviour continues; you've lost the ability to see it.

steps.p: Every safeguard has holes. So safety stacks several independent layers, so one failing isn't a disaster.
steps.analogy: Swiss cheese: each slice has holes, but stack enough and nothing gets straight through.

steps.p: Post-training teaches the model to refuse clearly harmful requests and be honest.
Separate classifier models screen what goes in and comes out for dangerous content, independent of the main model.
Red-teaming means people deliberately try to break the system before release, to find weaknesses.
If a model's parameters are public, anyone can fine-tune away its safety training, so only the training layer exists.

options: Deliberately trying to make it fail or misbehave, to find problems before release
Giving it to a rival team
cards.why: Attacking it on purpose. Better your own team finds the jailbreak than a stranger after launch.

cards.q: "Many-shot jailbreaking", described by Anthropic in 2024, works by…
options: Filling a long prompt with fake dialogues of an AI complying, then asking the real question
Asking politely many times in separate chats
cards.why: Flooding with examples. In-context learning cuts both ways: hundreds of fake "compliant" examples teach the model to comply.

cards.title: In Anthropic's 2025 bug bounty, no one found a universal jailbreak of its safety classifiers in over 3,000 hours of attempts.
cards.detail: The classifiers, trained on examples generated from a written constitution, screened inputs and outputs for dangerous content. Later public challenges did eventually find ways through.

cards.statement: If a model's parameters are public, its safety training can be removed by fine-tuning.
cards.why: True. A small amount of fine-tuning can undo refusals. That's a key trade-off in debates about releasing open models.

options: Layering several independent safeguards so one failure isn't catastrophic
Using only one very strong safeguard
cards.why: Many layers. Holes rarely line up across several independent slices, so harm has to get past every layer at once.

steps.p: Labs write down capabilities that would be dangerous — for example, meaningfully helping someone make a biological weapon.
Each new model is tested against those lines before it's deployed.
Crossing a line triggers tougher security and deployment rules. Anthropic calls these AI Safety Levels (ASL).
The EU AI Act puts extra duties on the largest general-purpose models, judged partly by how much computing trained them.
International reports, like one chaired by Yoshua Bengio in 2025, summarise what's known about AI risks for governments.

cards.q: In May 2025, why did Anthropic switch on ASL-3 protections?
options: As a precaution: it couldn't rule out that Claude Opus 4 crossed a chemical and biological risk line
Because it was required by law
cards.why: Precaution. Rather than wait for certainty, it applied the stronger safeguards when the line couldn't be ruled out.

cards.statement: The first International AI Safety Report, published in January 2025, was chaired by Yoshua Bengio.
cards.why: True. Bengio, a Turing Award winner and deep-learning pioneer, led around 100 experts from many countries.

cards.q: The EU AI Act presumes a general-purpose model poses systemic risk above what amount of training computing?
cards.why: 10²⁵ FLOPs. That's roughly the scale of the largest models around 2023. Above it, extra testing and reporting duties apply.

cards.title: In 2023, hundreds of AI researchers and lab leaders signed a one-sentence statement on extinction risk from AI.
cards.detail: Organised by the Center for AI Safety, it said reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.

cards.title: Read a system card
cards.body: Labs publish "system cards" with each major model: what it was tested for, what it can do, and what safeguards apply.
cards.challenge: Look up the system card for the AI assistant you use most and skim its safety section.
